title: More Condensate Secrets Revealed
body_text: I have a couple of papers to mention today that (to me, anyway) demonstrate how little we know about what’s going on with biomolecular condensates, the membraneless droplets that appear and disappear in every part of the cell. It’s only been in recent years that these have had the attention that they deserve, and I think it’s fair to say that we have a long way to go in understanding their properties and functions. This paper, for example, suggests that condensates in general have very strong effects on the solvation of particular amino acid side chains. The cationic ones have their protonated states stabilized, and the anionic ones have their neutral forms stabilized - everything shifts in the same direction. This effect doesn’t seem to be very sequence-dependent in these simulations, but it has to be said that the authors are looking mostly at “pure protein” phases in their models. Most real condensates seem to be mixtures of protein and RNA, but the general negative charge of those RNA molecules makes one think that this effect would persist in those condensates as well. Charge distribution is an important part of condensate formation and dissolution, and the distinct solvation properties of condensate interiors is crucial to their function. So it’ll be interesting to see if these effects can be backed up with more physical evidence. But it turns out that RNA molecules are not the only important nucleic acid constituent of condensates. This new paper finds that stress granules (which are a well-known condensate variety) have a good deal of circular DNA in them (of all things). In fact, more than half of the nucleic acid content in the stress granule cores can be circular, double-stranded DNA! This seems to have been missed in stress granule studies up until now, although the authors do reference a couple of papers which were on the track to make this discovery but didn’t go far enough. (Standard sequencing won’t pick these up, because they have no ends to work from!) It was already known that such granules contained DNA-binding proteins as well as RNA-binding ones, but these authors noticed that treating isolated stress granule cores with DNase I enzyme completely alters their morphology and behavior. By contrast, “plasmid-safe” DNase, which is known to not degrade circular double-stranded DNA plasmids, did very little to the cores. This holds true for both yeast and mammalian cells. Such extrachromosomal circular DNAs (eccDNAs) have been known for a long time, but their functions are much less well understood. One gets the impression that it’s been easier not to think about them, and that’s not the only cellular features you can say that about (biomolecular condensates themselves spent a long time in this category themselves!) It’s reminiscent of Douglas Adams’ “Somebody Else’s Problem” invisibility field from the Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy books. No definite cytoplasmic functions have ever been ascribed to them, at least not in vertebrates. The eccDNA species in stress granules do not appear to originate from mitochondria, in case you might be thinking that, and in fact they seem to cover the regular nuclear genome sequences fairly well. What’s more, there are actually a good number of histone-type proteins in the stress granule cores to keep them company. How that happens, and if they’re exported from the nucleus in this state, is unknown. There have been proposals that stress granule “seeds” are always present in the cytoplasm and that these species allow for rapid formation of the granules when they’re needed. It’s possible that these circular DNA molecules are a feature of these, but that remains to be proven. What their interactions with the RNA species in the granules are like is another mystery. But it won’t be the last of these condensate mysteries; I feel very confident saying that.
